summary: Gives offer/answer rules for the annexa parameter of G.723 and the annexb parameter of G.729, G.729D, and G.729E in SDP, for when the two sides give values that do not match.

eli5.summary: Two people setting up a call may disagree about a setting for sound compression. This document says what to do when their answers do not match.

questions: what happens if annexb does not match in sdp
sdp offer answer fmtp parameter mismatch
subtitle: What two phones should do when they disagree about silence suppression for G.723 and G.729 calls.

tldr.problem: The annexa (G723) and annexb (G729, G729D, G729E) parameters say whether voice activity detection is used, but the older specifications did not say what to do when the offer and answer carry different values. Implementations guessed differently, which led to a different codec being chosen or to call failure.
tldr.mechanism: A missing parameter counts as yes. If either side says no, the result is no. If the offer says yes and the answer says nothing, the result is yes.
tldr.outcome: Both sides now reach the same result for every combination, and the general aim is that Annex A or Annex B is not used if either side says it does not support it.

today: RFC 7261 is a Proposed Standard from May 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Mismatch Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4856 defines the annexa parameter for G723 and the annexb parameter for G729, G729D and G729E. Both indicate that voice activity detection (Annex A or Annex B) is used or preferred. The permissible values are yes and no, and yes is implied if the parameter is omitted.

The gap is what happens when the values differ in the SDP offer and answer. With an offer of annexb=yes and an answer of annexb=no, the pair could proceed as if the result were yes, or as if it were no. The existing specifications did not say, so implementations interpreted it in their own ways, resulting in a different codec being chosen or in call failure.

RFC 3264 requires SDP extensions that define new fmtp parameters to specify their interpretation in offer/answer. This document supplies that for annexa and annexb.
sections.eli5: Two people planning a call disagree about one setting, and nobody wrote down who wins. So different phone makers picked different winners, and some calls broke.

sections.title: The General Objective and Comfort Noise
sections.content:
The general objective is simple: if the offerer or answerer indicates it does not support Annex A or Annex B, then Annex A or Annex B is not used.

The RFC ties this to comfort noise frames. RFC 3551 says receivers MUST accept comfort noise frames if restriction of their use has not been signaled. So when an SDP offer or answer indicates that comfort noise is not supported, comfort noise frames MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: If anyone says 'please do not use the pause feature', nobody uses it. That keeps everybody happy.

sections.title: Rules for G723 Annex A
sections.content:
Because annexa is part of the original registration of audio/G723, all implementations that support G723 understand it. So when G723 appears with no annexa parameter, the case MUST be treated as annexa=yes.

  • Offer annexa=yes, answer annexa=no: both sides MUST proceed as if G723 is negotiated with annexa=no.
  • Offer annexa=no: after the exchange, both sides MUST proceed with annexa=no.
  • Offer with no annexa, answer annexa=yes: both sides MUST proceed with annexa=yes.

For the offer-says-no case, the RFC does not require the answer to repeat annexa=no, because some implementations omit the parameter in the answer. The result is still no.
sections.eli5: If nobody says anything, it counts as 'yes'. If one person says 'no', it is 'no', even if the other person forgets to repeat it.

sections.title: Rules for G729 Annex B
sections.content:
The rules for G729, G729D and G729E mirror the G723 ones, with annexb in place of annexa. In this section G729 stands for any of the three.

  • An absent annexb MUST be treated as annexb=yes.
  • Offer annexb=yes, answer annexb=no: both sides MUST proceed with annexb=no.
  • Offer annexb=no: both sides MUST proceed with annexb=no, even if the answer omits the parameter.
  • Offer with no annexb, answer annexb=yes: both sides MUST proceed with annexb=yes.
sections.eli5: The same 'any no wins, silence means yes' rule works for the other kinds of voice compression too.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three G729 examples, each using payload type 18 and G729/8000.

  • Offer annexb=yes, answer annexb=no: the result is annexb=no.
  • Offer annexb=yes, answer with G729 and no annexb: the result is annexb=yes, because the missing value means yes.
  • Offer with G729 and no annexb, answer annexb=no: the result is annexb=no.
sections.eli5: The examples are just practice questions. In each one, you check whether anybody said no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The only security guidance is a pointer: the guidelines in RFC 6562 for using voice activity detection (Annex A or Annex B) with the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) are to be followed.
sections.eli5: When a call is also scrambled for privacy, follow the safety advice from another document about pause detection.
